Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. - fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.

Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").

- review: Review a pull request

183	\paragraph{Diminishing returns of $N$-scaling.}
184	Our $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$ comparisons (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}) characterize the marginal value of additional samples for test-time scaling \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2024scaling}.
185	For quality estimation, structural signals benefit consistently but sublinearly: SJ $\rho$ improves by $+0.052$ (Qwen SciERC, 3-seed mean) and $+0.032$ (LLaMA CoNLL, 3-seed mean) when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, while log-probability is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta\rho{\leq}0.021$).

SJ, EM, and voting confidence scale consistently across all tested settings; only FK shows setting-dependent variation, suggesting that structural and binary-agreement signals are the most robust to $N$.

\paragraph{Cross-architecture transfer.}
LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct replicates the structural-over-surface ordering on SciERC NER (SJ $\rho{=}0.363$, FK $\rho{=}0.327$).
On CoNLL, the cross-architecture gap is minimal (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}): SJ achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ (LLaMA) vs.\ 0.436 (Qwen), $\Delta{=}0.005$.
At $N{=}16$, the structural-over-logprob advantage holds across all four tested settings: Qwen SciERC (Voting $\rho{=}0.411$ vs.\ logprob 0.259, $\Delta{=}{+}0.152$), Qwen CoNLL (EM $\rho{=}0.463$ vs.\ logprob 0.328, $\Delta{=}{+}0.135$), LLaMA SciERC (Voting $\rho{=}0.452$ vs.\ logprob 0.277, $\Delta{=}{+}0.175$), and LLaMA CoNLL 3-seed (SJ $\rho{=}0.463{\pm}0.007$ vs.\ logprob $0.310{\pm}0.005$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.153$).

\section{Calibration Analysis}\label{app:calibration}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_reliability}
\caption{Reliability diagrams on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Top: mean F1 vs.\ binned confidence; bottom: instance counts per bin. Left: NER; right: RE. NER signals are reasonably well-calibrated (calibration ECE 0.069--0.096), while RE shows greater miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339), reflecting the difficulty of calibrating confidence for compound extraction tasks.}
\label{fig:reliability}
\end{figure*}

NER signals are reasonably well-calibrated (calibration ECE 0.069--0.096), while RE exhibits greater miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339), indicating that translating consistency scores into calibrated confidence estimates is feasible for NER but remains challenging for compound extraction tasks.

\section{Additional Analyses}\label{app:additional}

\paragraph{Per-relation diagnostic.}
RE signal degradation is relation-specific.
\textsc{Feature-Of} has near-zero correlation ($\rho{=}0.004$), while \textsc{Hyponym-Of} achieves $\rho{=}0.646$.
The primary bottleneck is entity span errors, which account for 55.5\% of RE false negatives---a prerequisite failure that consistency signals cannot detect, as they measure agreement among equally incorrect extractions.
We note that RE analysis relies on a single dataset (SciERC); generalization to other RE benchmarks remains to be validated.

\paragraph{Capability stratification.}
For NER, SJ effectiveness scales with structural complexity: on SciERC instances with 6+ entities, $\rho{=}0.547$, compared to $\rho{=}0.415$ for 1--2 entities.
The SJ advantage over logprob remains stable across sentence-length quartiles ($\Delta\rho{\approx}0.08$--$0.20$).
For RE, SJ $\rho$ increases monotonically with sentence length (Q1: 0.110 $\to$ Q4: 0.473; Fisher $z$-test $p{=}0.004$), indicating that longer, more relation-dense sentences provide richer structure for consistency-based estimation.
Both proxies are weakly correlated with F1 ($|r|{<}0.15$), confirming they capture input complexity rather than directly predicting output quality; however, entity count and sentence length are themselves moderately correlated ($\rho{=}0.650$), so they reflect overlapping rather than independent complexity dimensions.
For RE, entity count and relation count are strongly correlated ($\rho{=}0.769$) and thus reflect a single structural complexity dimension rather than independent axes.
On the high-complexity RE subset ($n{=}81$, high relation count), signals improve substantially: Voting reaches $\rho{=}0.630$, logprob $\rho{=}0.554$, and SJ $\rho{=}0.502$---all far above the full-set levels.
Richer relational structure provides more signal for consistency-based estimation, complementing the task-level boundary established by WNUT-17: structural signals are most effective within a ``sweet spot'' of sufficient model capability and sufficient output complexity.

\paragraph{Length vs.\ log-probability.}
Figure~\ref{fig:length_logprob_scatter} shows that mean log-probability is weakly positively correlated with output length (NER: $\rho{=}0.386$, $n{=}4{,}232$; RE: $\rho{=}0.326$, $n{=}3{,}176$), ruling out length-penalty confounding as an explanation for logprob's selection failure: longer outputs receive \textit{higher}, not lower, token-averaged log-probability under constrained decoding.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig_length_logprob_scatter}
\caption{Output length vs.\ mean log-probability on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Positive correlations (NER: $\rho{=}0.386$; RE: $\rho{=}0.326$) rule out length-penalty confounding.}
\label{fig:length_logprob_scatter}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evaluation circularity.}
Leave-one-out SJ (LOO-SJ), which excludes the target sample when computing confidence, yields $\Delta\rho{=}{-}0.014$ relative to standard SJ (a correlation-level difference), with a maximum per-instance score difference of $3.1{\times}10^{-4}$ (negligible at the individual prediction level).
Evaluation circularity is negligible.

\paragraph{Conditional filtering details.}
On LLaMA conditional RE (non-zero F1 instances), SJ recovers to $\rho{=}0.405$ while FK drops to $\rho{=}0.259$, confirming that structural advantage is robust across both models and evaluation conditions.
At $N{=}16$, the divergence persists: SJ maintains $\rho{=}0.308$ on conditional RE while logprob drops to $\rho{=}{-}0.026$.
EM ranks first across all four tested conditional configurations---SciERC NER ($\rho{=}0.360$), CoNLL Qwen $N{=}16$ ($\rho{=}0.466$), CoNLL LLaMA 3-seed ($\rho{=}0.462$), and SciERC RE ($\rho{=}0.417$)---despite full-set rankings ranging from \#1 (CoNLL Qwen) to \#5 (SciERC RE).
On the full set, EM is diluted by trivial agreement: instances where all $N$ samples produce identical (possibly incorrect) outputs receive EM${=}1$ regardless of quality, compressing the signal's dynamic range.
On the conditional set---where the model demonstrably produces varied outputs---exact agreement becomes the strongest quality signal.
The margin over SJ is largest on RE ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.171$), where compound extraction decisions amplify output variability, and smallest on CoNLL LLaMA ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.002$), where all signals converge near $\rho{\approx}0.46$.

\paragraph{WNUT-17 full signal analysis.}
Table~\ref{tab:wnut} reports all five signals on WNUT-17.
Voting achieves $\rho{=}0.724$ (AUROC${=}0.913$) on the full set, but conditional analysis (non-zero F1 instances) reveals this is entirely driven by the zero/non-zero boundary: conditional $\rho{=}0.038$ ($p{=}0.49$).
Logprob shows the reverse pattern: full-set $\rho{=}{-}0.410$ but conditional $\rho{=}0.350$, the highest among all signals on the conditional set.
This inversion confirms that full-set correlations on high-failure-rate datasets conflate binary success prediction with quality gradation.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Quality estimation on WNUT-17 (Qwen, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, $n{=}689$ after filtering gold-empty instances). Cond: non-zero F1 instances ($n{=}334$). Logprob exhibits strong negative full-set $\rho$; its conditional $\rho$ reverses to the highest among all signals, confirming that full-set correlations on high-failure-rate datasets conflate binary success prediction with quality gradation.}
\label{tab:wnut}
\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
\toprule
Signal & $\rho$ & $p$ & AUROC & Cond.\ $\rho$ & Cond.\ $p$ \\
\midrule

Logprob & $-$.410 & ${<}$1e-28 & .219 & .350 & ${<}$1e-10 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Cross-configuration selection analysis.}
Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection} extends the selection analysis to four additional configurations.
On LLaMA SciERC, where output diversity remains substantial (18\% identical outputs, 39\% unique), logprob achieves the highest selection F1 (0.652) at $N{=}8$ but still falls within bootstrap noise of greedy (0.646), replicating the gap observed on Qwen SciERC (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
On CoNLL, 57--88\% of instances produce identical outputs across all $N$ samples, reflecting a ceiling effect (greedy F1 ${\approx}$0.91--0.92) rather than signal failure; selection analysis on these configurations is uninformative because there is little per-sample variance for any signal to exploit.

Best non-oracle signal per row in \textbf{bold}. No signal significantly outperforms greedy in any configuration; CoNLL shows especially tight clustering where greedy already exceeds 0.90.}
\label{tab:cross_selection}
\begin{tabular}{llccccccc}
\toprule
Config & $n$ & Greedy & Oracle & SJ & FK & EM & LP & VC \\
\midrule

LLaMA/SciERC $N{=}16$ & 529 & .645 & .806 & \textbf{.649} & \textbf{.649} & .640 & .646 & .640 \\

\paragraph{Diminishing returns of $N$-scaling.}
Our $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$ comparisons (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}) characterize the marginal value of additional samples for test-time scaling \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2024scaling}.
For quality estimation, structural signals benefit consistently but sublinearly: SJ $\rho$ improves by $+0.052$ (Qwen SciERC, 3-seed mean) and $+0.032$ (LLaMA CoNLL, 3-seed mean) when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, while log-probability is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta\rho{\leq}0.021$).
Structural signals leverage $\binom{N}{2}$ pairwise comparisons (28 pairs at $N{=}8$, 120 at $N{=}16$), but the $\rho$ improvement is far less than proportional, indicating diminishing information per additional comparison.
This asymmetry gives structural signals a relative advantage in the compute-constrained regime: at $N{=}8$, SJ already achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ on LLaMA CoNLL (vs.\ logprob $\rho{=}0.307$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.124$), and the gap \textit{widens} at $N{=}16$ ($\Delta{=}{+}0.153$) because structural signals continue to benefit from additional pairwise evidence while logprob does not.
For sample selection, additional samples increase the oracle upper bound---more draws raise the probability of a high-quality candidate---but signal-based selection remains flat because the selector's inability to identify the best candidate is a granularity limitation, not a sample size limitation.
The practical implication is that $N{=}8$ captures most of the achievable quality estimation benefit; further scaling widens rather than closes the correlation-selection gap absent stronger per-sample selectors.

Table~\ref{tab:bootstrap_signal_ci} reports bootstrap confidence intervals for individual signal $\rho$ and pairwise $\Delta\rho$ on SciERC NER ($N{=}8$, $n{=}529$, $B{=}10{,}000$, seed${=}42$).

The Voting--SJ gap ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.019$) is not significant, indicating that these two structural signals perform comparably.
The SJ--EM gap ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.065$) is borderline significant, with the CI lower bound at $+0.003$ and upper bound at $+0.130$.

Table~\ref{tab:diversity} summarizes output diversity across configurations.

\paragraph{Oracle-improvable fraction.}
Across SciERC configurations, 39--42\% of instances contain at least one sample with F1 exceeding greedy: Qwen NER 42.0\% (222/529, mean headroom $+$31.9~pp among improvable instances), Qwen RE 41.3\% (164/397, $+$45.3~pp), LLaMA NER 39.3\% (208/529, $+$33.7~pp).

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

This work provides, to our knowledge, the first multi-family comparison of confidence signals for test-time scaling in generative information extraction.
By comparing five signals from three families across NER and RE tasks of varying difficulty, we disentangle quality estimation from sample selection---two objectives that prior work has conflated.
Consistency-based signals are effective quality estimators ($\rho$ up to 0.38, AUROC up to 0.75), but we find no significant evidence that any signal surpasses greedy on best-of-$N$ selection on SciERC ($p{>}0.39$, 13--18~pp oracle headroom), a disconnect we term the \textit{correlation-selection gap}.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

This work provides, to our knowledge, the first multi-family comparison of confidence signals for test-time scaling in generative information extraction.
By comparing five signals from three families across NER and RE tasks of varying difficulty, we disentangle quality estimation from sample selection---two objectives that prior work has conflated.
Consistency-based signals are effective quality estimators ($\rho$ up to 0.38, AUROC up to 0.75), but we find no significant evidence that any signal surpasses greedy on best-of-$N$ selection on SciERC ($p{>}0.39$, 13--18~pp oracle headroom), a disconnect we term the \textit{correlation-selection gap}.
Signal rankings depend on task difficulty---exact match leads on easy tasks, structural signals on hard tasks---with this ordering consistent across model families.
While our NER findings are validated across three datasets, our RE conclusions rest on SciERC alone and warrant further validation.

Trained verifiers or reward models could close the selection gap by learning per-sample quality discrimination.
Cross-task transfer beyond IE, scaling to larger models (70B+), and integration with conformal prediction are promising directions.

\begin{abstract}
Test-time scaling through multi-sample generation promises quality improvements for LLM-based information extraction, but which confidence signals best serve quality estimation versus sample selection remains unclear.
We systematically compare five confidence signals from three families---structural (entity voting, Soft Jaccard), surface (exact match, Fleiss' $\kappa$), and model-internal (log-probability)---across NER (three datasets of varying difficulty) and RE (SciERC) with two model families (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B).
We find that the strongest signals achieve $\rho{=}0.38$ (entity voting) and AUROC${=}0.75$ (exact match) for quality estimation, with ranking and classification favoring different signals across task complexity; however, this strong quality estimation does not translate into selection gains---we find no statistically significant evidence that any signal surpasses greedy decoding on SciERC---where output diversity is substantial---across both model architectures ($p{>}0.39$, bootstrap) despite 13--18~pp of oracle headroom; on easier tasks, near-identical outputs preclude meaningful selection analysis.
We term this disconnect the \textit{correlation-selection gap}: instance-level consistency signals predict which inputs the model handles reliably, not which output is best among $N$ candidates.
Signal rankings further depend on task difficulty---exact match dominates easy tasks, structural signals dominate hard tasks, and when model capability is insufficient, apparent correlations are driven by zero/non-zero separation rather than genuine quality gradation---establishing that signal choice should be guided by task difficulty and intended application.
These results reframe consistency signals as quality estimators rather than output selectors for structured IE.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Self-consistency---sampling multiple outputs and aggregating them---has become a powerful strategy for improving language model reasoning.
On discrete-answer tasks such as arithmetic and commonsense QA, majority voting over chain-of-thought samples yields large gains: +18 percentage points on GSM8K (PaLM-540B; \citealp{wang2023selfconsistency}).
More broadly, test-time compute scaling through repeated sampling and selection has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling, offering substantial quality improvements at inference time \cite{snell2024scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
These results rest on a shared assumption: that among $N$ stochastic samples, a selection mechanism can identify better outputs.
For tasks with a single correct answer, this assumption holds naturally---the majority vote is the selector.
But information extraction (IE) poses a fundamentally different challenge.
The output is not a single token or number; it is a \textit{set} of entities or relations with internal dependencies, where two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical structures.
There is no obvious majority to vote on, partial agreement is the norm rather than the exception, and the space of valid outputs is combinatorially large.
Can self-consistency still provide useful signal in this structured setting?

Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated two distinct objectives: \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) and \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
These require fundamentally different signal properties: the former benefits from instance-level aggregation, while the latter demands per-sample discrimination.
Self-consistency methods for discrete answers \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc} and weighted variants \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence---an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
The most relevant study, \citet{nedellec2026consistency}, examines consistency--accuracy correlations for LLM-based IE, leaving open several questions that motivate our work: (i)~whether structural matching improves on their surface-level approach (which they acknowledge ``overlooks semantically consistent outputs''), (ii)~whether quality estimation translates to best-of-$N$ selection, and (iii)~whether findings generalize across a difficulty gradient beyond a single domain.
No existing work compares confidence signals from multiple families---surface-level, structural consistency, and probabilistic---for both quality estimation and sample selection in generative structured IE.

Our central finding is that consistency-based signals are effective quality estimators but poor sample selectors for structured IE.
Entity voting achieves $\rho{=}0.38$ on SciERC NER and exact match leads AUROC${=}0.75$, both practically useful for quality-aware routing.
Yet we find no statistically significant evidence that any signal surpasses greedy decoding on best-of-$N$ selection ($p{>}0.39$, bootstrap) despite 13--18~pp of oracle headroom.
We term this the \textbf{correlation-selection gap} (Figure~\ref{fig:overview}): instance-level signals predict \textit{which inputs} are hard, not \textit{which output} is best.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{The correlation-selection gap. Left: consistency signals (here entity voting) predict instance-level quality---high agreement correlates with high F1 ($\rho{\approx}0.38$, AUROC${\approx}0.69$). Right: the same instance-level signal assigns identical scores to all $N$ candidates from a given input, precluding sample selection. No signal significantly outperforms greedy on either task ($p{=}0.39$ for NER logprob; Table~\ref{tab:selection}).}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

We systematically evaluate five confidence signals from three families---structural (entity voting, Soft Jaccard), surface (exact match, Fleiss' $\kappa$), and model-internal (log-probability)---across NER and RE on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}, using Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B.

Our contributions are as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{A systematic multi-family comparison of confidence signals for generative IE.}
    We evaluate five signals from three families on quality estimation for NER and RE.
    Entity voting achieves the strongest $\rho{=}0.38$ while exact match leads AUROC${=}0.75$; signal rankings depend on both task complexity and evaluation metric, with structural signals leading rank correlation on complex schemas (SciERC) and surface signals leading on simpler tasks (CoNLL).

    \item \textbf{Identification of the correlation-selection gap.}
    We demonstrate a fundamental disconnect between quality estimation and sample selection in structured IE.
    Despite strong instance-level correlations ($\rho$ up to 0.38), we find no statistically significant evidence that any signal surpasses greedy on SciERC---where output diversity is substantial (39--43\% unique outputs)---across both model architectures ($p{>}0.39$, bootstrap) despite 13--18~pp of oracle headroom.
    This gap reflects the instance-level nature of consistency signals, which predict input difficulty rather than discriminating among individual samples.

    \item \textbf{Task-complexity boundary conditions.}
    Signal rankings depend on task difficulty: exact match leads on easy tasks (CoNLL), Soft Jaccard dominates on hard tasks (SciERC), and when model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17, 52\% zero F1), inflated full-set correlations collapse on the conditional set---all signals converge toward weak or non-significant correlations once the zero/non-zero boundary is removed.
    While our NER findings are validated across three datasets of varying difficulty, our RE conclusions are based on a single benchmark (SciERC) and warrant further validation.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
For per-instance quality ranking, entity voting provides the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$), though exact match leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.749$); under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$).
Signal rankings depend on task difficulty---EM dominates easy tasks (CoNLL), Voting and SJ dominate hard tasks (SciERC)---consistent across tested model families.
When model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17), all signals converge toward non-significant conditional correlations (Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).

\paragraph{Why the gap exists.}
Four of five signals are instance-level by construction and cannot rank $N$ candidates; the consensus-proximity strategy (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) adds no reliable value (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
Logprob, the sole per-sample signal, primarily reflects grammar compliance under constrained decoding---75\% of comparisons are effectively ties (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}).
The common root is that quality estimation ranks \textit{instances}, while sample selection ranks \textit{candidates within a single instance}, requiring per-sample quality information that neither instance-level aggregation nor token-level confidence provides.
On SciERC, diversity-stratified analysis confirms the gap persists even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}); calibration analysis shows RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}) may compound this failure.
These signals are thus well-suited for quality-aware routing but not for discriminating among candidates.

\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling}: SJ uses $U{=}\text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$, EM uses $U{=}\mathbb{1}[y_i{=}y_j]$ (standard majority voting), Voting uses entity-level overlap; each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$.
That all five MBR variants failed to surpass greedy reflects systematic utility-quality misalignment: these utility functions correlate with F1 at the instance level (AUROC up to 0.75) but fail to discriminate among candidates \textit{within} a single instance---the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.

\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
The decoupling of quality estimation ($\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) means evaluating on a single metric risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.
Effective selection likely requires per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers}; $N$-scaling analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:additional}) shows $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

This work provides, to our knowledge, the first multi-family comparison of confidence signals for test-time scaling in generative information extraction.
By comparing five signals from three families across NER and RE tasks of varying difficulty, we disentangle quality estimation from sample selection---two objectives that prior work has conflated.
Consistency-based signals are effective quality estimators ($\rho$ up to 0.38, AUROC up to 0.75), but we find no significant evidence that any signal surpasses greedy on best-of-$N$ selection on SciERC ($p{>}0.39$, 13--18~pp oracle headroom), a disconnect we term the \textit{correlation-selection gap}.
Signal rankings depend on task difficulty---exact match leads on easy tasks, structural signals on hard tasks---with this ordering directionally consistent across model families, though magnitudes are model-dependent.
While our NER findings are validated across three datasets, our RE conclusions rest on SciERC alone and warrant further validation.

Trained verifiers or reward models could close the selection gap by learning per-sample quality discrimination.
Cross-task transfer beyond IE, scaling to larger models (70B+), and integration with conformal prediction are promising directions.
